observations: The accessible-name mechanism for a frame element is the `title` attribute (WCAG technique H64), which this checklist treats under 2.4.1/4.1.2 below rather than here — 1.1.1's alt-text model applies to images/icons rendered by the component itself (as in ct-image/ct-video), not to a `<iframe>` whose own embedded document is opaque to this component.
Any audio/video played inside the embedded document is entirely outside ct-iframe's control — it has no visibility into, or ability to caption, the framed content.
Same boundary as 1.2.1 — captioning is the responsibility of whatever page/service is loaded at `url`, not this atom.

standard: 1.2.3 Audio Description or Media Alternative (Prerecorded) (Level A)

observations: ct-iframe renders a single `<iframe>` with no internal structure of its own (no headings, groups, or label associations) to misrepresent; structure inside the embedded document is out of scope.
ct-iframe has no input fields of its own; any form fields inside the embedded document are that document's responsibility.
Autoplaying audio (if any) originates from the embedded document, not from ct-iframe, which sets no audio/autoplay behavior itself.
The frame itself renders no text; `with-background`'s background-color/padding are decorative chrome around the embed, not text content requiring contrast.

When `width`/`height` are omitted the frame fills its container (`width: 100%`/`height: 100%`), so ct-iframe itself doesn't force a fixed-size viewport; whether the embedded document reflows at 320px is that document's own responsibility.

standard: 1.4.13 Content on Hover or Focus (Level AA)

observations: The `<iframe>` element is a native, always-focusable/tabbable element; ct-iframe adds no `tabindex` override and doesn't intercept keyboard events, so the frame is reachable via keyboard by default.

The single most iframe-specific keyboard concern: once focus moves inside the embedded document, whether Tab/Shift+Tab can move focus back out again is entirely determined by that document's own focus management — ct-iframe has no DOM access across the frame boundary to detect or prevent a trap. Compliance depends on the implementer only embedding third-party content known not to trap keyboard focus.
Any auto-updating/animating content (e.g. an embedded video autoplaying) is controlled by the embedded document, not by ct-iframe.

standard: 2.3.1 Three Flashes or Below Threshold (Level A)

observations: WCAG technique H64 (using the title attribute of frame/iframe elements) is the standard mechanism letting assistive-technology users identify a frame's purpose before deciding whether to enter it, functioning like a landmark to bypass/skip. ct-iframe exposes this via the optional `frameTitle` prop (native `title` attribute) — genuinely testable (axe's `frame-title` rule) but only enforceable when the implementer actually supplies a real, descriptive value; an omitted or empty title still renders a functioning but unlabeled frame.
ct-iframe renders a frame, not a page.
The frame occupies a single position in the host page's natural DOM/tab order (ct-iframe doesn't set `tabindex`); focus order *within* the embedded document is outside this component's boundary.
ct-iframe renders no link text of its own.
The mechanical 2.4.6 extractor evaluates `label`/`legend` text specifically; ct-iframe's closest analog, `frameTitle`, is covered under 2.4.1/4.1.2 above via `title`, not this SC.
ct-iframe's `static styles` set no `outline: none` or other focus-ring suppression on the `.ct-iframe` element, so the browser's native focus indicator remains visible when the frame receives focus.
Any gesture-based interaction happens inside the embedded document, not in ct-iframe's own (empty) pointer-event surface.
ct-iframe renders no visible text label alongside `frameTitle` for the two to conflict — `title` is the frame's only accessible name.
ct-iframe renders no clickable controls of its own outside the embedded document.
The embedded document declares its own `lang`, independent of the host page ct-iframe sits in.
Focusing the frame itself (before any interaction with its content) triggers no context change — ct-iframe attaches no focus handlers.
ct-iframe has no input controls of its own; `url`/`width`/`height`/`theme` are author-time configuration, not end-user input.
ct-iframe has no form validation of its own.
ct-iframe collects no user input.

The `<iframe>` element's implicit ARIA role already conveys "there is a frame here"; what's missing without a value is its accessible *name*. `frameTitle` (native `title` attribute) supplies that name and is checkable via axe's `frame-title` rule, but — same as every other optional accessible-name prop in this repo (`ct-button`/`ct-link`'s `aria-label`) — compliance depends on the implementer actually providing a real, descriptive value rather than leaving it unset.
ct-iframe has no dynamic status/live-region content of its own.
